clue.text: Death for him by knife and cord? Ay, together!

definitions.text: Death for him by knife and cord? Ay, together!

parts.words: Death for him by knife and cord? Ay, together!
parts.note: the French revolutionary stabbed in his bath; run 'cord' and 'Ay' together and you get Corday, the name of the woman who wielded the knife

explanation.surface: A grim riddle about someone killed by a blade and a rope, with an odd cheer at the end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Knife and cord' suggests stabbing plus strangling, but the cord is only half a name: joined to 'Ay' it gives Charlotte Corday, who knifed the revolutionary in 1793.
explanation.definitionFit: Charlotte Corday stabbed this French revolutionary journalist to death in his bath in 1793.

clue.text: A couple at sea getting spliced?

definitions.text: A couple at sea getting spliced?

parts.words: A couple at sea getting spliced?
parts.note: reads as two people marrying on a voyage, but a brace is a couple, the main is the sea, and 'splice the' this is the naval order for an extra tot of rum

explanation.surface: A pair of sweethearts getting married aboard ship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Splice the mainbrace' was the Royal Navy order to issue an extra ration of rum; the clue also hints at BRACE (a couple) and MAIN (the sea).
explanation.definitionFit: The brace on a ship's mainyard is the rope that the old naval phrase about a celebratory rum ration says to splice.

clue.text: William's plea for cover …

parts.note: a request to 'roof us' sounds like the nickname of William II of England, the red-haired son of the Conqueror

explanation.surface: Someone named William begging for shelter.
explanation.walkthrough: William II of England was known by a Latin nickname meaning 'red'; said quickly, 'roof us' is a plea for cover. The ellipsis carries the idea of cover on to the next clue.
explanation.definitionFit: William II, son of the Conqueror, was nicknamed for his ruddy complexion, and the nickname sounds like a request for a roof.

clue.text: … such as that Chinese dynasty can supply?

definitions.note: the ellipsis carries on from the clue before, so this means a cover such as a roof

parts.note: Ch'ing is the older spelling of Qing, the last imperial dynasty of China

explanation.surface: Continues the plea for cover: perhaps an old Chinese dynasty can provide the roofing.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition leans on 2-down: '… such as' means 'cover such as', and straw or reed roofing is exactly that. Ch'ing is the Wade-Giles spelling of the Qing dynasty.
explanation.definitionFit: Reed or straw roofing is a kind of cover for a house, so it continues the earlier clue's cover.

clue.text: Chess as an odd recreation for J. Bull in Glasgow

indicators.note: an odd re-creation means the letters of these words are made again in a strange new order

explanation.surface: Playing chess as an unusual pastime for an Englishman up in Scotland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Recreation' pretends to be a pastime, but read as re-creation it reshuffles CHESS AS AN. John Bull is the personification of England, and Glaswegians call the English by this Gaelic-derived name.
explanation.definitionFit: Scots use this slightly scornful word for an English person, and John Bull is the stock figure of England.

clue.text: Cheese won by Cambs from Hunts

definitions.text: Cheese won by Cambs from Hunts

parts.words: Cheese won by Cambs from Hunts
parts.note: the village that gave its name to a blue cheese moved from Huntingdonshire into Cambridgeshire, so Cambridgeshire took it from its neighbour

explanation.surface: A cheese prize carried off by one county's team from another's.
explanation.walkthrough: Cambs and Hunts are abbreviations for the English counties Cambridgeshire and Huntingdonshire; the village of this name was in Hunts until the 1974 boundary changes put it in Cambs.
explanation.definitionFit: The famous English blue cheese takes its name from a village once in Huntingdonshire and now in Cambridgeshire.

clue.text: Means of catching Junior, say, in a warm spot?

indicators.note: say signals that the phrase is only being spoken, so its sound and not its spelling matters

parts.note: a device to catch a son would be a son-trap

explanation.surface: Parents setting a snare for their boy somewhere warm.
explanation.definitionFit: A sheltered sunny corner of a garden that catches and holds warmth is a sun-soaked spot.

clue.text: Like the ogre's victim, vanquished, beheaded

indicators.note: beheaded tells us to lop off the first letter of the word for vanquished

parts.note: to be vanquished is to be beaten

explanation.surface: An ogre's prey, defeated and decapitated.
explanation.walkthrough: 'beheaded' removes the opening B from BEATEN.
explanation.definitionFit: Ogres in fairy tales devour their victims, so the victim has been consumed.

clue.text: It gives leave indeed to Albert to go free

annotationWithheld.why: It gives leave indeed to Albert to go free: the parse is QUIT (leave) in ACT (deed) + AL (Albert), but the single printed word 'indeed' must give both the insertion indicator 'in' and the fodder 'deed', one word doing two jobs
annotationWithheld.clue: It gives leave indeed to Albert to go free

clue.text: Last thing one does with boots, or cads

definitions.text: Last thing one does with boots
definitions.meaning: a cobbler working on a last finishes footwear by fitting the raised backs of the soles

explanation.definitionFit: Boots have raised backs fitted to their soles, often the final job on the cobbler's last; and rotters are called by the same word.

clue.text: Swell result of so much money about!

definitions.text: Swell result of so much money about!

parts.words: Swell result of so much money about!
parts.note: a swelling, and also what economists say happens to prices when too much money circulates

explanation.surface: Exclaiming how splendid it is to have so much cash around.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Swell' looks like slang for splendid, but it means a swelling, and too much money about causes prices to swell.
explanation.definitionFit: Blowing up something swells it, and a rise in prices from an excess of money is the economic sense.

clue.text: It goes ahead, to what outlandish end?

parts.note: que is French, an outlandish or foreign language, for what

explanation.surface: Someone asks what strange end something heading forward is going to.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It goes ahead' reads as a thing moving forward, but means a thing that goes on a head: a chef's or brimless hat.
explanation.definitionFit: A small brimless hat, such as a chef's tall white one, is worn on top of the head.

clue.text: Like backward gals in this English form

definitions.text: Like backward gals in this English form

parts.words: Like backward gals in this English form
parts.note: a simplified version of the language with a vocabulary of 850 words, as might suit slow girls in a school form

explanation.surface: A remark about slow pupils in a particular class at an English school.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Form' looks like a school class, but here it is a form of the language: C.K. Ogden's simplified English, a fit level for slow learners.
explanation.definitionFit: Ogden's simplified 850-word English bears this name, and it also means elementary or rudimentary.

clue.text: Maybe try Oakley's tough rules

indicators.note: maybe suggests the three letters could be arranged some other way

parts.note: Annie Oakley was the American sharpshooter, so her first name with a possessive

explanation.surface: Perhaps sample the stern regulations laid down by Oakley.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Maybe' rearranges TRY into TYR.
explanation.definitionFit: Despotic or oppressive regimes are harsh forms of government.

clue.text: Charge one thousand bucks to enter the island

indicators.note: enter means the next letters go into the middle of the island's name

parts.note: Arran is an island in the Firth of Clyde off western Scotland
the Roman numeral for one
a grand, a thousand dollars, is abbreviated G

explanation.surface: Someone is billed a thousand dollars to land on an island.
explanation.definitionFit: To bring a formal accusation against someone in court is to indict them.

clue.text: Bearing appears clear, even if complicated

indicators.note: if complicated tells us the letters of the two words are tangled into a new order

explanation.surface: A remark that a direction seems plain even when matters get tricky.
explanation.walkthrough: 'if complicated' rearranges CLEAR and EVEN.
explanation.definitionFit: A matter's bearing on a question is its pertinence or connection to it.

clue.text: Ian, so prudent when in Parliament

annotationWithheld.why: Ian, so prudent when in Parliament: 'prudent' defines it, but no wordplay from 'Ian, so ... when in Parliament' gives the letters, and the scan is too faint to show whether 'Ian' is misread
annotationWithheld.clue: Ian, so prudent when in Parliament

clue.text: Rooms booked up

parts.note: reads as hotel rooms all reserved, but means rooms filled with books

explanation.surface: A hotel that is fully reserved.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Booked up' sounds like no vacancies; it means stocked with books.
explanation.definitionFit: Rooms or buildings whose shelves hold collections of volumes for reading or lending.

clue.text: Edward, whose father was not ready, he admits

definitions.text: Edward, whose father was not ready
definitions.meaning: the Anglo-Saxon king Edward, son of Ethelred the Unready, had the epithet for his piety
one who admits his sins, or a priest who hears such admissions

explanation.definitionFit: King Edward, son of Ethelred the Unready, was known by this title, which also names one who acknowledges sins.

clue.text: Note clue about biblical king is pastoral

parts.note: E is one of the musical notes

indicators.note: about means the word clue is placed around the king's name

parts.note: Og was the king of Bashan in the Old Testament

explanation.surface: A clue about a king from the Bible turns out to be rural.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shout' is an OCR misreading of 'about'. Here 'pastoral' is a noun: a short poem about country life, not the adjective it seems.
explanation.definitionFit: A short poem about shepherds and rural life, like Virgil's, is a pastoral poem.

clue.text: Make Lords raise German capital in eel-processing

indicators.note: in places the turned-up city inside the processed letters
processing means the letters of eel are worked over into a new order
in a down clue raise means the city's name is read upwards, backwards

parts.note: Bonn was the capital of West Germany

explanation.surface: To be made a peer, lift a German city into an eel factory.
explanation.walkthrough: Bonn was West Germany's capital until reunification; in a down clue 'raise' reads it upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: To raise someone to the peerage makes them a noble, so the verb fits creating lords.

clue.text: Mischievous demon captures oriental tapestry

indicators.note: captures means the demon holds the next letter inside it

parts.note: a goblin is a mischievous sprite
E for east, the Orient

explanation.surface: An impish sprite seizes a wall-hanging from the East.
explanation.definitionFit: The Paris workshop of this family name produced famous woven wall-hangings.

clue.text: Ballet girls' leader, is she French?

indicators.note: the leader of the word girls' is its first letter

parts.note: elle is French for she

explanation.surface: Asking whether the girl leading a ballet troupe is French.
explanation.walkthrough: The ballet is Adolphe Adam's Romantic work of 1841.
explanation.definitionFit: A Romantic ballet by Adam about a peasant girl who dies of a broken heart.

clue.text: Welsh devil of the deep blue sea?

definitions.text: Welsh devil of the deep blue sea?

parts.words: Welsh devil of the deep blue sea?
parts.note: sailors' name for the evil spirit of the ocean, whose surname is a common Welsh one

explanation.surface: Asking about a demon from Wales who lives in the ocean.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Between the devil and the deep blue sea' is the idiom; the sailors' devil of the sea bears the most Welsh of surnames.
explanation.definitionFit: Sailors' folklore names the spirit of the sea bed, whose locker holds drowned men, with a Welsh first name and surname.

clue.text: What the judges said

parts.note: Latin plural for authoritative pronouncements, including judges' remarks

explanation.definitionFit: Judicial pronouncements, especially remarks made in passing, are known by this Latin plural.

clue.text: A marine sort of boat

definitions.meaning: naval slang for a Royal Marine
a small ship's boat used for general work

explanation.definitionFit: Sailors nicknamed a Royal Marine this way, and a ship's small working boat has the same name.

clue.text: Pace is slow, blame injury

definitions.note: the clue phrase describes a walk at a leisurely pace, a verb phrase for the noun or verb

indicators.note: injury suggests the word blame is damaged, its letters knocked out of order

explanation.surface: A hurt makes someone walk slowly, and they blame the injury.
explanation.walkthrough: 'injury' rearranges BLAME.
explanation.definitionFit: A stroll at an easy, leisurely gait is a slow walk.

clue.text: Top dressing available from any barber etc

indicators.note: available from means the letters can be found inside the run of words that follows

explanation.surface: A hair treatment you can get at any barber's shop.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Top dressing' looks like a hair product; it is clothing for the top of the head, a flat soft cap.
explanation.definitionFit: A soft round flat cap is something worn on the head.

clue.text: Is a novice able to make way for ships?

parts.note: to be able is to can, the modal verb
L for learner, as on a learner driver's plate

explanation.surface: Asking if a beginner is good enough to clear a path for vessels.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Is ... able' gives CAN, with 'a novice' (A L) after it.
explanation.definitionFit: An artificial waterway cut for boats and ships.

clue.text: Among poets, the two way Italian game

indicators.note: among means the Italian letters sit inside the word for poets

parts.note: bards are poets
il is Italian for the, and written both ways it reads IL then LI

explanation.surface: Among the poets, an Italian game played both ways.
explanation.walkthrough: IL (Italian 'the') written forwards and then backwards gives ILLI.
explanation.definitionFit: A cue sport played with balls on a cloth-covered table.

clue.text: A light gas

parts.note: reads as a gas of low weight, but means a gas burnt to give light, as in old lamps

explanation.definitionFit: This hydrocarbon was burned in lamps for illumination and in welding torches.

clue.text: Stray perhaps through the woods to see him ?

definitions.text: through the woods to see him
definitions.note: you would roam the forest to meet this goat-legged figure, a phrase for the noun

indicators.note: perhaps suggests these letters could be arranged differently

explanation.surface: Wander through the forest to find a woodland figure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' rearranges STRAY.
explanation.definitionFit: A goat-legged woodland deity of Greek myth roams the forests.
